title: Concurrency patterns that tie it all together
goal: By the end you can name the concurrency patterns behind your services (producer-consumer, worker pool, thread-per-message, active object, guarded suspension, balking, read-write lock, future), and build and test a circuit breaker and a fail-fast bulkhead that combine State, Decorator and compare-and-set.

warmup.q: A service on virtual threads handles each incoming payment in its own virtual thread and calls a card issuer that allows 50 concurrent requests. A traffic spike brings 5,000 payments at once. What protects the issuer?
options: Nothing is needed: virtual threads are cheap, so 5,000 calls are fine
The JVM limits virtual threads to the number of CPU cores
A semaphore bulkhead of 50 around the issuer call
A larger heap
warmup.why: Virtual threads remove the cost of threads, not the limits of what they call. Thousands of them will happily send thousands of concurrent requests. The JVM runs them on a few carrier threads, but a blocked virtual thread unmounts, so all 5,000 can be waiting on the issuer at once. A bulkhead (a semaphore with `tryAcquire`) caps the in-flight calls at what the issuer allows.

sections.h: Circuit breaker: State, Decorator and compare-and-set in one class

figure.caption: The breaker's three states. Only one probe runs in half-open; its result decides whether the breaker closes or opens again.

analogy: Picture a restaurant kitchen. The order rail is producer-consumer: waiters clip tickets on, cooks take them off, and a full rail tells the waiters to slow down. Each station has four burners, so a run on soup can't take the grill's burners: a bulkhead. When the fryer catches fire, someone hangs a sign saying "no fried food for ten minutes", and orders that need it are refused at the door instead of waiting forever: the breaker opening. When the dishwasher is already running, nobody starts a second one: balking. The analogy breaks on knowing why. A kitchen can see the fire. A breaker only counts failures, so you must tell it which errors mean "the dependency is sick" and which, like a declined card, mean the dependency is working perfectly.
in_your_world: Your Kafka consumers are producer-consumer at the scale of a cluster: partitions are the queues, and a consumer per partition is the confinement that keeps per-account ordering safe. Your Quarkus services already speak these patterns through SmallRye Fault Tolerance's `@CircuitBreaker`, `@Bulkhead`, `@Retry` and `@Timeout`, which are interceptor-based, so they need calls that go through the proxy. Temporal brings its own retry policy for activities: don't add a second retry around the PSP call inside the activity, or one failure becomes nine calls. And breakers are per instance: with six pods, each pod has its own breaker and its own view of the issuer, so the fleet keeps probing a dead issuer six times as often as one pod would.
mistake: The most common mistake is retrying at every layer. The mobile app retries three times, the API gateway retries three times, the payment service's client retries three times, and Temporal retries the activity. One user tap becomes dozens of calls to an issuer that is already struggling, and the retries keep it down. It happens because each team adds a retry to make their own layer reliable, and nobody sees the product. Retry in one place, close to the call, only for idempotent operations or with an idempotency key, with backoff and jitter. Never retry a `CallNotPermitted` or a full bulkhead: those mean "stop", not "try again".

compare.title: Guarded suspension: waiting for a 3-D Secure callback

java.title: ChallengeResults.java

kotlin.title: ChallengeResults.kt

compare.note: Both replace the hand-written `wait()` in a `while` loop with a one-shot promise, which can't miss a signal or wake up spuriously: `complete` happens once, and `get` or `await` returns as soon as it has. The difference is what waiting costs. `CompletableFuture.get` blocks a thread; on a virtual thread that is cheap, but it is still a thread per waiting payment. `CompletableDeferred.await` suspends the coroutine and holds no thread at all, and `withTimeout` cancels the wait cleanly. Java needs three checked exceptions in the signature; Kotlin needs none, and the timeout arrives as a `TimeoutCancellationException`. One gap is shared: a callback that arrives after the waiter gave up leaves an entry in the map, so a real version also expires old entries.

worked.title: Put retry, breaker and bulkhead in the right order

steps.say: Three pieces from this lesson wrap one PSP charge. The order of the wrappers decides what happens on a bad day. Before reading on: with retry outermost, what does each retry attempt do while the breaker is open?
steps.code:
Supplier<String> charge = () -> psp.charge("order-7781:charge", "tok_42", 1_250);   // idempotency key

Supplier<String> limited = () -> bulkhead.call(charge);       // innermost: caps the calls in flight to the PSP
Supplier<String> guarded = () -> breaker.call(limited);       // then: stop calling a PSP that keeps failing
String ref = retrying(3, guarded);                            // outermost: try again on transient failures
steps.alt_code:
val charge = Supplier { psp.charge("order-7781:charge", "tok_42", 1_250) }   // idempotency key

val limited = Supplier { bulkhead.call(charge) }              // innermost: caps the calls in flight to the PSP
val guarded = Supplier { breaker.call(limited) }              // then: stop calling a PSP that keeps failing
val ref = retrying(3) { guarded.get() }                       // outermost: try again on transient failures

steps.say: Each attempt hits the open breaker and gets `CallNotPermitted` in microseconds, which costs the PSP nothing. But a rejection isn't a transient failure, and retrying it is noise. Teach the retry to let fail-fast signals through untouched.

Why is the bulkhead inside the breaker? An open breaker rejects before the bulkhead is reached, so a dead PSP never holds permits. Why is the retry outside? Each attempt is a separate breaker call, so three failed attempts count as three failures, and a PSP that is really down trips the breaker within one or two payments. Retrying inside the breaker would hide those failures from it.
steps.code:
what each layer sees for one payment while the PSP returns 503:

retry      attempt 1          attempt 2          attempt 3
breaker    Closed(0) -> (1)   Closed(1) -> (2)   Closed(2) -> Open    (three failures trip it)
bulkhead   permit, released   permit, released   permit, released

next payment: retry -> breaker rejects at once (CallNotPermitted) -> no PSP call, no permit

steps.say: Pin it in a test with a fake PSP that always fails and the lab's classes. The second payment must never reach the PSP.
steps.alt_code:
val pspCalls = AtomicInteger()
val failing = Supplier<String> { pspCalls.incrementAndGet(); throw IllegalStateException("PSP 503") }
val breaker = CircuitBreaker(3, Duration.ofSeconds(30), clock)
val bulkhead = Bulkhead(20)
val pipeline = { breaker.call { bulkhead.call(failing) } }

assertThatThrownBy { retrying(3, pipeline) }.hasMessage("PSP 503")                      // 4. first payment: 3 attempts
assertThat(breaker.state()).isInstanceOf(CircuitBreaker.Open::class.java)
assertThatThrownBy { retrying(3, pipeline) }.isInstanceOf(CircuitBreaker.CallNotPermitted::class.java)
assertThat(pspCalls.get()).isEqualTo(3)                                                 // 5. the second never left

lab.title: A circuit breaker with a fake clock, and a semaphore bulkhead
steps: Read the state table in the Javadoc of `CircuitBreaker`; the states, the constructor and `state()` are given. Run the tests: all ten fail.

Write the first half of `call`: read the state. If it is `Open` and the clock is still before `until`, throw `CallNotPermitted`. If the cool-down is over, `compareAndSet` it to `HalfOpen`, and throw if you lose. If it is already `HalfOpen`, throw.

Write the second half: run `op`. On success, move to `Closed(0)` unless another thread has opened the breaker meanwhile. On a `RuntimeException`, apply the failure transition with `updateAndGet` and rethrow the same exception.
Run the tests until all ten pass, then run them twice more. Concurrency code has to pass every time.
hints: `if (s instanceof Open(var until))` gives you `until` in one step. `state.compareAndSet(s, new HalfOpen())` succeeds only if nobody changed the state since you read `s`, so exactly one thread becomes the probe.
On success, `state.updateAndGet(cur -> cur instanceof Open ? cur : new Closed(0))` closes both a half-open breaker and a closed one with failures, without undoing an open set by another thread.
The failure transition is the four-case `switch` from the lesson: `HalfOpen` and the tripping `Closed` both become `new Open(clock.instant().plus(openFor))`.
lab.done_when: All ten tests in `ResilienceTest` pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: A fail-fast bulkhead from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a `Bulkhead` that lets at most `n` calls run at once and rejects the rest immediately with an exception. Then answer two questions: what goes wrong if you `release()` outside a `finally`, and what changes if you use `acquire()` instead of `tryAcquire()`?

alt.title: Kotlin

recap: Producer-consumer: share a bounded queue and nothing else. One poison pill per consumer in Java; `close()` the channel in Kotlin, and use `for`, not `consumeEach`, in each worker.
Thread-per-message is back with virtual threads and coroutines, but cheap threads make it easy to flood a dependency, so it always comes with a limit.
Balking returns at once when the object is busy. Use `compareAndSet` (or `Mutex.tryLock`), never a check-then-act on a plain boolean, and remember it only covers one JVM.
A bulkhead is a semaphore per dependency with `tryAcquire`: it fails fast, releases in `finally`, and is sized to the dependency, not to your threads.
A circuit breaker is State plus Decorator plus compare-and-set: sealed states in an `AtomicReference`, a `call(op)` wrapper, an injected `Clock`, and one half-open probe chosen by `compareAndSet`.
Retry in one layer only, around idempotent calls, outside the breaker, and never on `CallNotPermitted` or a full bulkhead.

quiz.q: A Java pipeline has four consumer threads reading a `BlockingQueue`. After the last job, the producer puts a single `Stop` pill, then calls `close()` on the executor. What happens?
options: All four consumers stop, because they all see the pill
One consumer stops and the other three keep processing new jobs
One consumer stops, three block in `take()` forever, and `close()` never returns
The queue throws because a pill was taken twice
quiz.why: `take()` removes the pill, so exactly one consumer sees it. The other three wait for the next item, which never comes, and `ExecutorService.close()` waits for them. Put one pill per consumer, or in Kotlin close the channel, which ends every `for` loop.

quiz.q: A Quarkus service on virtual threads calls an issuer that allows 50 concurrent requests. Which limit fits best?
options: A semaphore of 50 around the issuer call, with `tryAcquire` so extra calls fail fast
A fixed pool of 50 platform threads for the whole service
No limit: virtual threads are cheap
A new `CompletableFuture` per call
quiz.why: The limit belongs to the dependency, not to the service's threads, and with virtual threads a semaphore is the natural way to express it. A fixed pool of 50 throttles everything the service does, not just the issuer calls. "Virtual threads are cheap" is exactly how you send 5,000 requests to an issuer that takes 50.

quiz.q: In a unit test, a Resilience4j 2.4.0 circuit breaker built with the default config fails five calls in a row, yet it stays `CLOSED`. Why?
options: Resilience4j only counts checked exceptions as failures
The default `minimumNumberOfCalls` is 100, so the failure rate isn't calculated yet
Breakers only open after `waitDurationInOpenState` has passed
The test needs a real clock
quiz.why: With the defaults, the breaker needs at least 100 recorded calls before it computes a failure rate, so five failures change nothing. Set `minimumNumberOfCalls` and `slidingWindowSize` to small numbers in tests. All exceptions are recorded by default, and `waitDurationInOpenState` controls how long it stays open, not when it opens.

quiz.q: A scheduled reconciliation job can also be started by an operator. If a run is already in progress, a second trigger should simply return. Which pattern is this?
options: Guarded suspension
Read-write lock
Producer-consumer
Balking
quiz.why: Balking means: if the object isn't in the right state, return at once instead of waiting. Guarded suspension is the opposite, waiting until the condition holds, which here would queue a second run behind the first. Implement it with `compareAndSet` on an `AtomicBoolean`, and with a database lock or lease if it must be unique across pods.

quiz.q: From *Atomics and compare-and-set*: when the cool-down ends, many request threads find the breaker `Open` with an expired `until` at the same moment. Why must the move to `HalfOpen` be a `compareAndSet` rather than a plain `set`?
options: `set` is slower than `compareAndSet`
So exactly one thread wins the right to probe; with `set`, every thread that saw the expired state would probe the PSP
`AtomicReference` doesn't allow `set` on records
`compareAndSet` makes the PSP call atomic
quiz.why: Each thread read the same `Open` state. `compareAndSet(open, halfOpen)` succeeds for the first thread only, because after that the state is no longer the `Open` object the others read, so their CAS fails and they're rejected. A plain `set` lets all of them through to a PSP that may still be down. CAS makes the state change atomic, not the call itself.

flashcards.back: A full bounded queue makes producers wait, which is backpressure. An unbounded one hides overload until memory runs out.

flashcards.front: N consumers stop on poison pills. How many pills?
flashcards.back: N, one per consumer: each `take()` removes one pill. In Kotlin, `close()` the channel instead.

flashcards.front: Balking or guarded suspension: which returns at once?
flashcards.back: Balking returns immediately if the object is busy. Guarded suspension waits until the condition holds.
`tryAcquire`, so a call over the limit fails fast. `acquire` waits in line, which makes it a limiter. Release in `finally` either way.

flashcards.front: Circuit breaker: what happens in each state?
flashcards.back: Closed: calls pass and failures are counted. Open: calls are rejected at once. HalfOpen: one probe runs; success closes, failure reopens.
100. A default breaker in a unit test that fails a handful of calls never opens.

flashcards.front: Which exceptions should a retry wrapper never retry?
flashcards.back: Fail-fast signals such as `CallNotPermitted` and a full bulkhead, and anything non-idempotent sent without an idempotency key.

terms.plain: Producers put work on a shared queue and consumers take it off; the queue does the locking and waiting.
A special message that tells one consumer to stop.
An object whose method calls become messages run one at a time by its own thread, returning futures.
Returning at once instead of waiting when the object isn't in the right state, such as "already running".
Waiting until a condition holds, then going on; `wait` in a loop, or a future.
A per-dependency cap on concurrent calls, so one slow dependency can't use up everything.
A wrapper that stops calling a failing dependency for a while, then probes to see if it recovered.
The breaker state after the cool-down, where one probe call decides whether to close or reopen.

explain_back.prompt: Explain how the lab's circuit breaker combines State, Decorator and compare-and-set, and why the move from open to half-open has to be a `compareAndSet`.
explain_back.answer: The breaker's state is a small sealed type, `Closed(failures)`, `Open(until)` and `HalfOpen`, and each outcome moves it with a pure transition, like the payment state machine. That's State. Its `call(op)` takes any operation and returns that operation's result through the same shape, adding behavior around it, which is what a decorator does. The current state lives in an `AtomicReference` so that hundreds of request threads can share one breaker without a lock, and every change is a compare-and-set or `updateAndGet`. The open-to-half-open move matters most. When the cool-down ends, many threads may read the same expired `Open` state at once. `compareAndSet(thatOpen, new HalfOpen())` succeeds for exactly one of them, which becomes the probe; the others see their CAS fail and are rejected. With a plain `set`, every one of them would probe a PSP that may still be down. The injected `Clock` is what lets the tests check all this without sleeping.

deeper.body:
Resilience4j's breaker defaults, read from its source and printed by version 2.4.0: `failureRateThreshold` 50%, `slowCallRateThreshold` 100%, `slowCallDurationThreshold` 60 s, `waitDurationInOpenState` 60 s, `permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState` 10, `minimumNumberOfCalls` 100, and a count-based sliding window of 100 calls. Every exception counts as a failure unless you configure `recordExceptions` or `ignoreExceptions`. The project's README says Resilience4j 3 will require Java 21 and adds virtual-thread schedulers; it wasn't on Maven Central when this course was written, so the labs build the breaker by hand.

Spring Framework 7 added `@Retryable` and `@ConcurrencyLimit` to the core framework, switched on with `@EnableResilientMethods`. `@Retryable` defaults to `maxRetries = 3` after the first failure, so four attempts in total, with a one-second delay. Both work through proxies, so the self-invocation rule applies.

Structured concurrency is the future-and-promise pattern with a lifetime. `StructuredTaskScope` forks subtasks, joins them, and cancels the rest when one fails, so no subtask outlives the method that started it. It is still a preview API in JDK 25, 26 and 27 (run with `--enable-preview`), which is why it stays out of the labs. Kotlin's `coroutineScope` has worked this way since the start: an `async` that fails cancels its siblings, and the scope waits for every child.

The patterns in this lesson have distributed cousins. A database row lock or a lease is balking across pods. Kafka partitions are producer-consumer with ordering per key. A Temporal workflow is an active object with durable state: one logical thread per workflow, commands in, results out. The questions you ask stay the same: who owns the state, what waits, and what fails fast.
